definition: Document classification or document categorization is a problem in library science, information science and computer science.
details: The task is to assign a document to one or more classes or categories. This may be done "manually" (or "intellectually") or algorithmically. The intellectual classification of documents has mostly been the province of library science, while the algorithmic classification of documents is mainly in information science and computer science. The problems are overlapping, however, and there is therefore interdisciplinary research on document classification. The documents to be classified may be texts, images, music, etc. Each kind of document possesses its special classification problems. When not otherwise specified, text classification is implied. Documents may be classified according to their subjects or according to other attributes (such as document type, author, printing year etc.). In the rest of this article only subject classification is considered. There are two main philosophies of subject classification of documents: the content-based approach and the request-based approach.

explainer.lead: Document classification is the task of putting a document into one or more categories, either by human judgement or by an algorithm. It provides a shared problem for library science, information science and computer science, with text classification usually meant unless another kind of document is specified.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a pile of papers into labelled trays, such as one for sports and one for science. Document classification means doing that sorting for documents, and a paper can go into more than one tray when it fits several labels. A person can make the decisions, or a computer can follow an algorithm.
tiers.practitioner: Apply document classification by defining the categories, deciding whether a document may receive several of them, and choosing manual or algorithmic assignment. Text is the default case, but images and music bring their own classification problems. For subject classification, distinguish a content-based approach, which uses what the document is about, from a request-based approach.
tiers.paperLevel: Given a document d and a set of classes C, the task is to assign d to one class or to a subset of C. Classification may be intellectual or algorithmic, and documents may be texts, images, music or other kinds, each with its own problems. Subject classification follows either a content-based or a request-based philosophy, while classification can instead use attributes such as document type, author or printing year.

explainer.example: A text document about a football match could be assigned to the class “Sports”; if the scheme allows multiple classes and another relevant label applies, it could receive that label too.

explainer.intuition: The idea is to give each document a useful label, or several labels, according to a chosen classification scheme. Those labels can describe its subject or another attribute, such as its type, author or printing year.
howItWorks: Choose the documents and the classes or categories to use.
Decide whether each document belongs to one class or may belong to several.
For subject classification, choose a content-based or request-based approach.
Assign the classes manually or algorithmically, using methods suited to the document kind.
explainer.whyItMatters: It turns document collections into classified collections through either human intellectual work or algorithms. Because these traditions overlap, the problem encourages research across library science, information science and computer science.
misconceptions: It is not limited to text: images and music can also be classified, although text classification is implied when nothing else is specified.
A document does not always receive exactly one category; the task allows one or more classes.
Classification is not always by subject: attributes such as document type, author and printing year can also be used.
